A tiny static-site generator for people who think in folders.
Field Notes turns a folder of Markdown into a fast, linkable site with zero config. No front-matter rituals, no build pipeline to babysit — your directory structure is the site map.

Most static-site generators ask you to learn their world before you can publish a paragraph. Field Notes flips that: point it at a folder, and the folder is the site. Sub-directories become sections, file names become URLs, and back-links are discovered automatically.

It's a single Go binary with no dependencies to install and no JavaScript shipped by default. Builds of a few hundred pages finish in well under a second, which keeps the write-save-refresh loop feeling instant.

> Your directory structure is the site map.

Keeping the surface area small is the entire design philosophy. Every feature request gets weighed against the question: does this earn its place, or does it just make the tool harder to hold in your head?

Annotate anything you read on the web — keep only the notes that matter.
Margin is a browser extension for people who read to think. Highlight a passage on any page and it's saved — clean, searchable, and yours — without a heavyweight read-it-later account behind it.

I read a lot on the web and kept losing the good parts. The bookmarks pile up, the read-later queue becomes a graveyard, and the one sentence I actually wanted is gone. Margin started as a weekend tool to fix exactly that for myself.

The whole thing runs locally. Highlights live in IndexedDB, sync is opt-in, and the popup is a fast index you can search by word, domain, or date. No feed, no streaks, no nudges to come back. The goal is to help you finish reading, not to keep you reading.

> The goal is to help you finish reading, not to keep you reading.

The hardest part was making highlight anchoring survive the messy reality of the web — pages that re-render, lazy-load, and rewrite their own DOM. I landed on a layered approach: a precise text-quote anchor first, a structural fallback second, and a graceful "orphaned note" state when a page changes out from under you.

A calmer way to read the news — no infinite feed, just one daily edition.
Tidal delivers one edition a day and then stops. It's a deliberate antidote to the endless scroll — a finite, beautifully set stack of stories you can actually get to the bottom of.

Every news app I tried was a slot machine. Tidal asked a simpler question: what if the news had an ending? You get one edition each morning, you read it, and you're done. The app literally tells you when you've finished.

I owned the interface end to end — type system, motion, the edition's card stack, and the reading view. SwiftUI let me move fast on a custom layout that still felt native: a spring-free, ease-out page turn and a typographic reading mode tuned for long sittings.

> What if the news had an ending?

Restraint was the whole product. The hardest design calls were all subtractions — no badge counts, no trending tab, no "because you read". What's left is quiet, and people stay longer because of it, not in spite of it.

A colour-contrast checker that lives in your menu bar.
Prism is a menu-bar pipette that samples any two pixels on screen and tells you, instantly, whether the contrast passes WCAG. Built for designers who check ratios a hundred times a day.

Checking contrast meant leaving my design tool, pasting hex codes into a website, and squinting at a pass/fail badge. Prism collapses that into a keystroke: pick two colours anywhere on screen and read the ratio in the menu bar.

It samples real screen pixels with Core Graphics, so it works against anything — a live website, a mockup, a photo. The whole UI is one popover: two swatches, the ratio, and the AA/AAA verdicts for normal and large text.

> A focused tool, retired the moment the platform made it redundant.

Prism is archived now — the system colour-picker caught up and I'd rather point people there than maintain a tool the OS made redundant. I'm leaving it up because the source is a tidy little example of a focused AppKit utility.

In praise of tools that do one thing
The best software I've made was the software I refused to add features to.
The best software I've made was the software I refused to add features to. Here's what saying no kept teaching me.

Every tool I've built has faced the same gravitational pull: do more. Add the integration, the dashboard, the second mode, the settings screen for the settings screen. The requests are always reasonable in isolation. It's the sum that quietly ruins things.

A tool that does one thing can be held entirely in your head. You know what it's for, you know its edges, you trust it not to surprise you. The moment it does two things, you have to start remembering which mode you're in, and the cognitive cost lands on every single use forever after.

> Saying no is a design skill, not a personality trait.

Saying no is a design skill, not a personality trait. It means having a sharp enough sense of what a tool is for that you can tell a good feature from a merely plausible one. Most features are plausible. Very few are good.

The tools I still use years later are almost all small. They didn't grow into platforms. They stayed exactly what they were, did it well, and earned a permanent place precisely because they never asked me to relearn them.

Most apps are designed to never let you finish. I think the opposite is worth designing for.
Most apps are designed to never let you finish. I've spent a few years building the opposite, and I want to make the case for software that's content to let you leave.

There's a quiet assumption baked into most of the software we use: that more engagement is always better. More time in the app, more sessions per day, more notifications answered. It's so common that we've stopped noticing it. But engagement is a means, not an end, and somewhere along the way a lot of products forgot which was which.

Calm software starts from a different premise. It assumes you have somewhere better to be. Its job is to help you do a thing and then get out of your way — to have an ending. A calm app tells you when you're caught up. It doesn't manufacture urgency it doesn't actually feel. It treats your attention as borrowed, not owned.

> A calm app treats your attention as borrowed, not owned.

This is harder to build than it sounds, because almost every default cuts the other way. The frameworks make infinite lists trivial and endings hard. The analytics dashboards reward the metrics that calm software deliberately suppresses. You end up writing more code to do less, and explaining to people why the number that went down is the point.

But the payoff is a particular kind of trust. When a tool respects your time, you reach for it without that low hum of dread. You let it into your day because you know it won't overstay. That trust compounds, quietly, in a way no growth loop ever will.

I don't think every product can or should be calm. But far more could be than currently are, and the ones that try tend to be the ones people genuinely love. That seems like a trade worth making.

I write to find out what I think
A short note on why this site has a writing section at all.
A short note on why this site has a writing section at all — and why I keep coming back to it even when no one's reading.

I don't write because I've figured something out. I write because I haven't, and the writing is how the figuring happens. A vague intuition stays vague until I'm forced to put it in order, sentence after sentence, and discover where it falls apart.

This is why the writing here sits next to the work, not in some separate blog. The essays and the projects are the same activity in two registers — both are me trying to think clearly about how software should feel, one in prose and one in code.

> I don't write because I've figured something out. I write because I haven't.

Most of these pieces are unfinished thoughts, and that's the point. If I waited until I was sure, I'd never publish anything. So I publish the figuring-out, and sometimes a reader writes back with the part I was missing.
